pr_title: extmod/modbluetooth_nimble: Clarify active state and check state for most ops.
pr_body:
Extension of #5638 (ensure that the BLE stack is active before allowing various operations). Also hopefully fixes #5686 (BLE stack state not reset across soft reset).

Compared to #5638, I've pushed this into the stack bindings because it gives a bit more flexibility for the stack to decide how to manage its state. Also clarifies the state better (adding the "stopping" state), and renames `mp_bluetooth_is_enabled` to the more self-explanatory `mp_bluetooth_is_active`.

The ESP32 port was missing a call to `mp_bluetooth_deinit` which I think explains #5686. I wasn't able to repro the crash while waiting for the result, but I was able to get a family of related crashes to @codefreax's findings about invoking a bad callback, due to invalid stack state. i.e. start scan, soft reset, then while sitting at the REPL post-reset, it crashes as nimble tries to handle an incoming HCI packet.
pr_comments: You also need to protect the call to `ble_hs_id_copy_addr()` in `mp_bluetooth_get_device_addr()` — this is where I had the crash on ESP32.

nit: Theoretically, even the call to `ble_gap_adv_active` in `mp_bluetooth_gap_advertise_stop` must be protected because it could use uninitialized memory. Only when looking into the implementation it becomes clear that the memory is in BSS and everything works as expected.
Does `gattc_on_data_available` have to be protected, too, for the same reasons `gap_event_cb` is protected?

Thanks for this.  I've rebased it on latest master which includes BTstack and tested it on 2x PYBD; it works.  I also made the errno easily configurable via the macro `ERRNO_BLUETOOTH_NOT_ACTIVE` and set it to `MP_ENODEV` for now (can be changed later if there's something better).

Merged in 1937fb22abc8e6192f6acfc037f2e9fd59fc6d8c
Note: I did not merge the esp32 change, that's now in a separate commit bd746a46309efc261d6124b546b5bf6775d47460

issue_context.title: ESP23 - Scanning Bluetooth Characteristics results in Kernel Panics
issue_context.body:
Hello,

I have modified some bluetooth code to read the characteristics of a xiamoi flower meter (hardcoded a mac address for my first tests). I can scan the devices and list the services using the interrupt method described in the documentation. But as soon as I try to retrieve the characteristics I get a kernel panic.

This is the code I use:
```
import time
import bluetooth
import binascii
from micropython import const

_IRQ_CENTRAL_CONNECT                 = const(1 << 0)
_IRQ_CENTRAL_DISCONNECT              = const(1 << 1)
_IRQ_GATTS_WRITE                     = const(1 << 2)
_IRQ_GATTS_READ_REQUEST              = const(1 << 3)
_IRQ_SCAN_RESULT                     = const(1 << 4)
_IRQ_SCAN_COMPLETE                   = const(1 << 5)
_IRQ_PERIPHERAL_CONNECT              = const(1 << 6)
_IRQ_PERIPHERAL_DISCONNECT           = const(1 << 7)
_IRQ_GATTC_SERVICE_RESULT            = const(1 << 8)
_IRQ_GATTC_CHARACTERISTIC_RESULT     = const(1 << 9)
_IRQ_GATTC_DESCRIPTOR_RESULT         = const(1 << 10)
_IRQ_GATTC_READ_RESULT               = const(1 << 11)
_IRQ_GATTC_WRITE_STATUS              = const(1 << 12)
_IRQ_GATTC_NOTIFY                    = const(1 << 13)
_IRQ_GATTC_INDICATE                  = const(1 << 14)

def bt_irq(event, data):
    if event == _IRQ_CENTRAL_CONNECT:
        conn_handle, addr_type, addr = data

    elif event == _IRQ_CENTRAL_DISCONNECT:
        conn_handle, addr_type, addr = data

    elif event == _IRQ_GATTS_WRITE:
        conn_handle, attr_handle = data

    elif event == _IRQ_GATTS_READ_REQUEST:
        conn_handle, attr_handle = data

    elif event == _IRQ_SCAN_RESULT:
        addr_type, addr, connectable, rssi, adv_data = data
        print(addr)
        if addr == b'\xc4|\x8df\xdd\xf0':
            print(data)
            bt.gap_connect(addr_type, addr, 2000)

    elif event == _IRQ_SCAN_COMPLETE:
        pass

    elif event == _IRQ_PERIPHERAL_CONNECT:
        conn_handle, addr_type, addr = data
        bt.gattc_discover_services(conn_handle)

    elif event == _IRQ_PERIPHERAL_DISCONNECT:
        conn_handle, addr_type, addr = data

    elif event == _IRQ_GATTC_SERVICE_RESULT:
        conn_handle, start_handle, end_handle, uuid = data
        if str(uuid) == "UUID16(0xfef5)":
            bt.gattc_discover_characteristics(conn_handle, start_handle, end_handle)

    elif event == _IRQ_GATTC_CHARACTERISTIC_RESULT:
        conn_handle, def_handle, value_handle, properties, uuid = data
        print(data)

    elif event == _IRQ_GATTC_DESCRIPTOR_RESULT:
        conn_handle, dsc_handle, uuid = data

    elif event == _IRQ_GATTC_READ_RESULT:
        conn_handle, value_handle, char_data = data

    elif event == _IRQ_GATTC_WRITE_STATUS:
        conn_handle, value_handle, status = data

    elif event == _IRQ_GATTC_NOTIFY:
        conn_handle, value_handle, notify_data = data

    elif event == _IRQ_GATTC_INDICATE:
        conn_handle, value_handle, notify_data = data

bt = bluetooth.BLE()
bt.active(True)
bt.irq(handler=bt_irq)
bt.gap_scan(10000, 10000, 10000)

time.sleep(20)
```

With all of these, the key value to look for is EXCVADDR - the virtual address that caused the exception. If it is something like 0x00000004 then it is a fair bet that this is an offset from a NULL pointer.
If you use the traceback information and find the code where the error occurred, it may well have a function call (perhaps BLE_GATTC_RX_EXTRACT_RX_ENTRY) that returns a pointer (such as 'rx_entry') that shortly after is used to call a 'callback' function. [See one of the early posts in this thread for an example.]
It so happens that the callback address is at offset 0x00000004 in the struct being pointed to. However if the pointer is NULL then it will try to access the low address referenced in EXCVADDR.
Until the original source code gets fixed, all you can really do is to test the pointer and only use it is not NULL.
